Overview

The term differential diagnosis refers to both the process of, and end product of, taking in all the information from a patient in front of you and synthesizing a set of possible diagnoses that are likely.

The differential diagnosis (ddx) is important because we can never be too certain a given diagnosis explains a patient’s clinical presentation.

It is also important because it gives us an existing framework to modify what we use as the working diagnosis as new information comes in (e.g new symptoms, CT scan findings, labwork).

In this article we will provide an approach for developing a ddx and frameworks for organizing your thinking around possible explanations of a given clinical presentation.

An Approach to the Differential Diagnosis

A 58 year old man with a 8 year history of osteoarthritis presents to you with a 2 day history of epigastric pain and malena. The patient does endorse alcohol use. The patient is otherwise well aside from the osteoarthritis.

While this clinical vignette is short, the purpose is to outline how one would approach creating a ddx.

A ddx consists of four fundamental parts

  • A list of potential diagnoses
  • Aspects which make it more likely for a diagnosis to explain the presentation
  • Aspects which make it less likely for a diagnosis to explain the presentation
  • The relative rank likelihood that a given diagnosis explains the presentation (this is a function of the above two parts)

Let’s walk through the above clinical vignette using these fundamentals.

Potential Diagnoses

This is the broadest part of the process. This list is generated by considering what could cause the presenting symptoms/signs. For the sake of illustration, we will consider a non-comprehensive list of potential diagnoses.

  1. Peptic Ulcer Disease
  2. Stomach Cancer
  3. Esophageal Variceal Bleeding

Aspects which make a given diagnosis more likely

Now, we must consider aspects of the clinical presentation which make a given diagnosis more likely. Another critical aspect of this step is to consider the prevalence of a diagnosis (e.g., peptic ulcer disease is much more common than a vascular malformation).

Let’s walk through each diagnosis and examine what makes each diagnosis more likely.

Peptic Ulcer Disease

  • Peptic ulcer disease is common
  • Peptic ulcer disease causes GI bleeding which explains the malena and activates visceral pain signals in the stomach which explains the epigastric pain
  • The patient has osteoarthritis, NSAIDs are a first-line treatment for this condition and these also cause thinning of the gastric lining, making one more susceptible to peptic ulcer disease
  • The malena suggests that there is GI bleeding, coming from a proximal source.
  • The onset of symptoms is acute

Stomach Cancer

  • Stomach cancer can cause GI bleeding, which manifests as malena in this patient
  • The expansion of a tumour into the surrounding viscera (e.g. stomach, gallbladder) can cause epigastric pain

Esophageal Variceal Bleeding

  • Distended varices can cause GI bleeding, which manifests as malena in this patient
  • The activation of visceral pain receptors in the esophagus can cause epigastric pain.

Aspects which make a given diagnosis less likely

Stomach Cancer

  • Stomach cancer is relatively rare
  • There are no reported malignancy-associated symptoms (e.g., weight loss, night sweats)
  • Acute presentation; stomach cancer symptoms tend to manifest more chronically
  • No mass effect symptoms of a tumour (e.g., early satiety)

Esophageal Variceal Bleeding

  • Variceal bleeding tends to occur in those with portal hypertension, a likely cause is cirrhosis but the patient does not endorse alcohol use.
  • Variceal bleeding tends to produce a large volume of blood which presents as hemetemesis which is not present in this patient

Relative Ranking of Diagnoses

Given the above pertinent features which make the diagnoses more and less likely, we can rank the differential diagnoses by how likely each one is.

Given that peptic ulcer disease has many ‘more likely’ factors and no ‘less likely’ factors, it is our most likely diagnosis.

Both stomach cancer and variceal bleeding are both unlikely given the ‘more’ and ‘less’ likely features. Clinically, a more in depth history and physical would be needed. However given the chronicity of symptoms and the lack of malignancy and mass effect symptoms, we will rank variceal bleeding as more likely than stomach cancer.

The process of creating the relative ranking early on in the process is difficult given the lack of information, however it helps guide which investigations to order and how to interpret the results of those results.

So, here is our current ranking of which diagnoses are most likely:

  1. Peptic Ulcer Disease
  2. Variceal Bleeding
  3. Stomach Cancer

This process has given us an idea of what our working diagnosis is, if there are any immediate treatments we should consider and how we should guide additional history taking, physical exam and investigations going forward. Once those are determined, it gives us an existing framework to update with new information.

Frameworks

While we provided a truncated list of potential diagnoses, there are many more diagnoses that could be considered. Furthermore, how does one generate these diagnoses in the first place? That is where frameworks can help us generate diagnoses.

Below, we present a framework often used to generate potential diagnoses based on presenting symptoms and complaints.

Framework: VITAMIN CDE

  • V: Vascular
  • I: Infectious and/or Inflammatory
  • T: Traumatic and/or Toxic
  • A: Autoimmune or Anatomic Variant
  • M: Metabolic
  • I: Iatrogenic or Idiopathic
  • N: Neoplastic
  • C: Congenital
  • D: Degenerative
  • E: Endocrine and/or Environmental

Note: it is often best to consider congenital causes more so in pediatric patients because this is when their first presentation will likely be. However adults can have their first presentation of congenital issues and children can have many other causes to their presenting illnesses.

Summary

The differential diagnosis is a powerful tool for structuring clinical thinking around a presenting patient. We hope this article helped shed some light around its value and how to create your own differential diagnosis!
